# Down-Sampling {#sec-imbalenced-downsample}

::: {style="visibility: hidden; height: 0px;"}
## Down-Sampling
:::

Downsampling is one of the conceptually easiest ways to handle imbalanced data.
Like all other methods in this section, it is a supervised method,
since it requires knowledge of the outcome.
This also means that it can only be applied to the training data set,
since we need the outcome.
See also [up-sampling](imbalenced-upsample.qmd), which is the opposite action.

The algorithm is quite simple.
Tally the number of observations within each class, as well as keep track of which observations are associated with each class.
The class with the fewest observations is then denoted as the minority class,
The remaining classes are denoted as the majority classes.
The observations of each majority class are then sampled without replacement to decrease the number of observations in the class.
Typically, to align with the number of observations with that of the minority class.

One could also modify this for a different threshold,
say 300%, which would make all majority classes with more than 300% of the number of observations of the minority class,
downsample until they have at most 300% of that of the minority class.

When using downsampling we are deleting data completely.
And there is a definite risk that we are throwing away the signal when we do this.
This is even more drastic when we have a sharp imbalance between the majority and minority classes.
Having a 99-1 split in the data would have you remove 98% of the data set, which is not a wise choice.

## Pros and Cons

### Pros

- Computationally fast and simple.

### Cons

- This could give issues if there is a big imbalance, causing us to remove almost all the data.
- Solves tasks that could be better handled with other methods.

## R Examples

```{r}
#| label: ames
#| echo: false
#| message: false
set.seed(1234)
```

We will be using the same subset of the `ames` data set as in the [up-sampling](imbalenced-upsample.qmd) chapter.

```{r}
#| label: show-data
#| message: false
library(recipes)
library(themis)
library(modeldata)
library(dplyr)
data("ames")

ames_imbalance <- ames |>
  filter(MS_Zoning %in% c("Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density")) |>
  mutate(MS_Zoning = droplevels(MS_Zoning)) |>
  select(MS_Zoning, Lot_Area, Year_Built, Gr_Liv_Area, Full_Bath)

ames_imbalance |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

{themis} provides `step_downsample()`, which has the implementation for down-sampling.

```{r}
#| label: step_downsample
downsample_rec <- recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_downsample(MS_Zoning)

downsample_res <- downsample_rec |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL)

downsample_res |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

Both classes now match the size of the smallest class.
Note how much data this threw away: we went from 2735 rows down to 924, discarding close to two thirds of the data set.

It includes the `under_ratio` argument to only partially update the data set.
Setting it to `2` allows the majority class to stay twice as large as the minority class.

```{r}
#| label: step_downsample-under_ratio
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_downsample(MS_Zoning, under_ratio = 2) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

## Python Examples

```{python}
#| label: python-setup
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from sklearn import set_config

set_config(transform_output="pandas")
pd.set_option('display.precision', 3)
```

We are using the same subset of the `ames` data set as above.

```{python}
#| label: show-data-py
from feazdata import ames

ames_imbalance = ames[ames["MS_Zoning"].isin(
    ["Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density"])]

X = ames_imbalance[["Lot_Area", "Year_Built", "Gr_Liv_Area", "Full_Bath"]]
y = ames_imbalance["MS_Zoning"]

y.value_counts()
```

{imblearn} provides `RandomUnderSampler()` for down-sampling.

```{python}
#| label: randomundersampler
from imblearn.under_sampling import RandomUnderSampler

X_res, y_res = RandomUnderSampler(random_state=1234).fit_resample(X, y)

y_res.value_counts()
```

The `sampling_strategy` argument serves the same purpose as `under_ratio` does in {themis}, but it is specified the other way around.
Where `under_ratio = 2` lets the majority class stay twice the size of the minority class, the equivalent here is the minority-to-majority ratio of `0.5`.

```{python}
#| label: randomundersampler-sampling_strategy
X_res, y_res = RandomUnderSampler(
    sampling_strategy=0.5, random_state=1234).fit_resample(X, y)

y_res.value_counts()
```
